name: Geolocation in iframes
plain: Lets an embedded frame ask for location only if the parent page allows it.
meaning: Controls whether ad, map or widget frames can see where the person is. The default blocks cross-origin frames so third parties cannot request location through a host page.

access.prompt_ui: Same prompt as top-level, worded for the top-level site; the grant is delegated to the iframe origin.
access.persistence: Per top-level origin; delegated frames share the top-level grant
access.revocation: Same site settings entry as the top-level origin
access.iframe: Default allowlist is self. Cross-origin frames need allow on the tag; a header of geolocation=() disables it for everyone.
steps: Browser checks the policy chain then the permission
Prompt or silent result per stored decision

chrome.note: Feature Policy 60, allow attribute 64, header renamed Permissions-Policy in 88

safari.note: allow attribute honored, header support partial

limits.headline: Can let an embedded map ask for your location, only if the host page allows
limits.user_action: You tap Find me or Use my location inside an embedded map or widget
can: Ask for location from inside an embedded frame, if the host page lets it
Show a prompt that names the main site
Give the embedded map your position after you allow it
cannot: Ask for location by default when it comes from a different site; that is blocked
Get location without the host page's permission setting
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Firefox support it fully. Safari support is partial.

story.what_it_is: Decides whether an embedded ad, map or widget on a page may see your location.

marketing.name: Permissions Policy
marketing.pitch: Describes a way for a page to allow or block features like location for embedded frames.

story.for_you: You may see a location prompt that names the main site, not the embedded widget. By default, third party frames cannot ask at all. You usually never notice this protection working.
story.for_makers: Maps, store finders and ads are often embedded from another company. The page owner must explicitly allow location for them, which keeps other companies from watching you through an ad frame.

use_cases.example: A restaurant page embeds a map from Google and allows location so it can show your route.
A retailer allows its own store finder frame to use location, but not an ad frame.
An ad network frame would love to know your location, but is blocked unless the site says yes.
A booking page allows a map widget to use location for 'near me' listings.
A game on a portal page in an embedded frame cannot see location unless the portal lets it.
A site blocks location in all embeds to keep ad fraud and spying away.

technical_bounds: Cross-origin frames cannot request location by default
Policy cannot grant more than the person granted
Sandboxed frames without allow-same-origin may fail

abuse: Hidden ad frames requesting location when a publisher sets allow="geolocation *"

history.change: Feature Policy header introduced with a geolocation feature
Header renamed from Feature-Policy to Permissions-Policy
